title: Marmalade Pudding
subtitle: Steamed sponge with a bitter-sweet marmalade base
excerpt: A steamed sponge pudding with a layer of Seville orange marmalade at the base. Turned out at the table, the marmalade becomes the glossy, bitter-sweet sauce that coats the top.
sourceNotes: A close cousin of the golden syrup sponge from Mrs Beeton. The marmalade variant became a standard winter pudding in British cookery after Seville oranges became widely available in the early 19th century. The technique is identical to a golden syrup pudding; only the base changes.

content.text: Marmalade pudding is a steamed sponge with Seville orange marmalade at its base, turned out to reveal the glossy, bittersweet top. The sponge is light and yielding; the marmalade sets to a sticky, fragrant sauce as it heats through. It steams for 1 hour 30 minutes and is best served the moment it is turned out, with pouring custard or a little warm cream.

Grease a 1-litre pudding basin generously with butter. Spoon the marmalade into the base and spread it as evenly as you can. The marmalade does not need to be perfectly level, it will spread as the pudding steams.

Beat the butter and sugar together until pale and fluffy. Add the beaten eggs a little at a time, beating well after each addition. If the mixture curdles, add a spoonful of flour and it will come back together. Fold in the flour, then the milk, to give a soft dropping consistency, the batter should autumn from the spoon in a slow, even drop.

Spoon the sponge batter over the marmalade and smooth the top gently. Cut a circle of baking paper and a piece of foil, both slightly larger than the top of the basin. Grease the paper on the underside. Place the paper over the basin, then the foil on top. Make a pleat in the centre of both to allow for expansion. Tie securely around the rim with string, and make a string handle across the top so you can lower and lift the basin safely.

Lower the basin into a large pan. Add enough boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the basin. Cover the pan with a lid and steam over a medium-low heat for 1 hour 30 minutes. Keep the water at a steady, gentle simmer and top it up with boiling water whenever it drops below halfway. Do not let the pan boil dry.

Lift the basin from the pan and rest for 2 minutes. Remove the foil and paper. Run a palette knife or the blade of a round-ended knife around the inside edge of the basin to loosen the sponge. Place a warm serving plate over the basin and invert quickly and confidently, hesitating causes the sponge to stick. Serve immediately with custard or pouring cream.

items.symptom: The sponge sticks to the basin
items.cause: The basin was not greased thoroughly, or the pudding was left to cool before turning out.
items.fix: Grease every part of the inside surface next time. Always turn out while still hot. A brief warm on the outside of the basin with a hot cloth will help release a stuck pudding.

items.symptom: The sponge is undercooked in the centre
items.cause: The steam was not consistent, or the basin is wider than 1 litre.
items.fix: Return the basin to the pan and steam for a further 20 minutes. Test by inserting a skewer, it should come out clean.

items.symptom: The marmalade has spread into the sponge
items.cause: This is normal. The marmalade softens and rises slightly into the sponge during steaming.
items.fix: Nothing to fix, the flavour distributes into the sponge as it should. The marmalade layer on top will still be visible and glossy when turned out.

content.text: Best eaten immediately after turning out. Leftovers can be refrigerated for up to 2 days, covered. Reheat individual portions by steaming in a covered bowl over simmering water for 15 minutes, or in a microwave with a damp sheet of kitchen paper over the top.
